ex = mf.example()
st = mf.spatial_story()
kp, beta = ex["kp"], ex["beta"]

Kriging predicts a field as a mean field plus a GP anomaly. Where floats are sparse the anomaly
reverts to zero and the map falls back on the mean field, so a mean field fitted to preferentially
sampled profiles carries their bias into the gaps. This report compares three fits of the mean
field on the toy jet of [the toy report](simex.qmd), each followed by the same kriging step.

## Toy with a seasonal cycle

The field is the Bickley-jet OHC plus a seasonal cycle that is stronger in the north,
$$
Z(x,y,t) = \underbrace{-\tanh(y/L) + a(y)\cos\!\big(2\pi(t-t_0)/365\big)}_{\mu(y,t)} \;+\; \eta(x,y,t),
\qquad a(y) = 0.3\,\big\{1+\tfrac12\tanh(y/L)\big\},
$$
with $\eta$ the eddy part of the jet streamfunction. $\eta$ has zonal mean zero, so the box mean is
$\bar Z(t) = \int Z(\cdot,t)\,d\mathbb P = 0.3\cos\{2\pi(t-t_0)/365\}$ exactly. The seasonal term
is thermal only; the flow, including the weak drift toward warm water, is unchanged.

Sixty floats are deployed uniformly on day $0$. After a one-year spin-up, $4$ years of $10$-day
profiles give $146$ snapshots and $8{,}760$ profiles per replicate. In the example replicate below,
`{python} f"{(prof.y < 0).mean():.0%}"` of profiles are in the warm southern half, and within a
latitude band they also favour warm eddies: the anomaly $\eta$ averages
`{python} f"{eta_prof:+.3f}"` at the profiles against $0$ over the box.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Z in the warm and cold seasons with that snapshot's floats, and the box mean through the record."
_show_fig(mf.plot_setup(ex))
```

## Three mean fits

All three fits use the same basis $h(y,t)$: a cubic in $u = y/250$ km, the annual harmonics, and
the harmonics times $u$ (so the seasonal amplitude can vary with latitude). The cubic does not
contain $\tanh$, so the mean is approximated, as in a real local window. The third fit adds
$\log\hat q_t(x,y)$, where $\hat q$ is the stacked cloud density from anchors $4$ cycles back (as in
the toy report), relative to uniform and floored at $0.05$.

| fit | coefficients | intuition |
|---|---|---|
| OLS, no $\hat q$ | $\hat\beta = (H^\top H)^{-1}H^\top z$ | every profile is one vote |
| GLS, no $\hat q$ | $\hat\beta = (H^\top K^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top K^{-1}z$ | correlated profiles share a vote |
| GLS + $\log\hat q$ | as GLS, with $\log\hat q$ as an extra column of $H$ | crowded water is allowed to be warmer |

$K$ is the anomaly covariance at the profiles: block diagonal by year (years as i.i.d. replicates),
anisotropic exponential in $(x,y,t)$ with a $10^{-3}$ relative nugget. Its parameters are *oracle*
values, the $e$-folding scales of the true $\eta$
($\ell_x = `{python} f"{kp['lx']:.0f}"`$ km, $\ell_y = `{python} f"{kp['ly']:.0f}"`$ km,
$\ell_t = `{python} f"{kp['lt']:.0f}"`$ d), so that only the mean-field step differs between fits.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Example replicate. Left: zonal mean of each fitted mean field against the true mean field on one cold-season day. Middle: latitude distribution of all profiles (dashed: uniform). Right: box mean of each fitted mean field alone, against the truth."
_show_fig(mf.plot_fits(ex))
```

OLS lets the crowded south and its warm eddies dominate, and its mean field runs warm in both
halves of the box, most of all in the sparse north. GLS treats a cluster of nearby profiles as fewer
independent votes, which removes the warm offset in the south but leaves much of it in the north. The $\log\hat q$ column lets the fit attribute the extra warmth of crowded water to the
crowding itself ($\hat\gamma = `{python} f"{beta['glsq'][-1]:.2f}"`$ here), so where $\hat q$ is
typical or low the mean is not pulled warm. The $\hat q$ column also shifts the latitude
coefficients, because $\hat q$ itself varies with latitude; $\hat\gamma$ is therefore not an
interpretable effect, only part of a better prediction.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Left: expected float density q-hat on one day. Right: the true anomaly eta, with the contour where q-hat is twice uniform. Floats are expected where eta is warm."
_show_fig(mf.plot_q_term(ex))
```


## Three estimators of the box mean

**Kriging.** Each fitted mean field is followed by simple kriging of the residuals,
$$
\hat Z_{\mathrm{K}}(t^*) \;=\; \int \hat\mu(\cdot,t^*)\,d\mathbb P \;+\; \sum_i w_i\,\big\{Z_i - \hat\mu(x_i)\big\},
$$
with block-kriging weights $w_i$ from all profiles within $\pm 30$ d of $t^*$. The weights depend
only on the profile positions and $K$, so they are the same for the three fits; only the residuals
differ.

**Cross-fit DR, leave one float out.** For each float $f$, the map $\hat m^{(-f)}$ is the mean
fit plus kriging computed without any of float $f$'s profiles. In its GLS + $\log\hat q$ fit, the
covariate comes from the other floats' clouds only. The pooled $\hat q$ at a time after $t^*$ is
anchored partly on float $f$'s own positions near $t^*$, so using it would let float $f$'s realized
position into the map that float $f$ checks. With $q_f$ the cloud density of float $f$ (expected
profiles per km$^2$), $q = \sum_f q_f$ the stacked density, and $|\mathcal X|$ the box area,
$$
\hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}(t^*) \;=\; \int \sum_{f}\frac{q_f}{q}\,\hat m^{(-f)}\,d\mathbb P
\;+\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal X|}\sum_{f}\sum_{i\in f}\frac{Z_i - \hat m^{(-f)}(x_i)}{q(x_i)}\,\mathbf 1_{C}(x_i),
$$
where $C = \{q\,|\mathcal X|/n \ge 0.05\}$ is the covered set. Off $C$ the $n$ maps are averaged
with equal weight and no correction is made. The map term is not the full-data map. Each float's
own influence on the map is removed in proportion to where that float was expected to be, which is
what keeps a float from checking a map it helped build. Floats move independently given the flow.
Conditional on the other floats, Campbell's theorem gives
$\mathbb E\sum_{i\in f} g(x_i) = \int g\,q_f\,d\mu$, so if the clouds' density were exact,
$$
\mathbb E\big[\hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}(t^*)\big] - \bar Z(t^*) \;=\; -\int_{C^c}\Big(Z - \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_f \mathbb E\,\hat m^{(-f)}\Big)\,d\mathbb P .
$$
This is an exact identity, with a positivity remainder on the uncovered set only. With estimated
densities $\hat q_f$ the bias picks up the product term
$\sum_f\int (Z-\hat m^{(-f)})(q_f-\hat q_f)/\hat q\,d\mathbb P$. Under the correct cloud model, that
error comes only from Monte Carlo and kernel smoothing in $\hat q_f$ ($200$ particles per cloud,
$10$ km bandwidth) and from binning to the $5$ km grid. On average $C$ covers
`{python} f"{dc.cover.mean():.1%}"` of the box.

The DR step is applied to all three mean fits. Estimates are taken at every third snapshot of each
of `{python} df.rep.nunique()` replicates. The $60$ leave-one-out kriging maps share one
cross-covariance per target. Each needs only the solve
$K_{-f}^{-1}\,(Z-\hat\mu^{(-f)})$, so leave-one-float-out costs little more than a single map.

## One day, map by map

The figures below follow the example replicate through one cold-season day (day
`{python} f"{st['t']:.0f}"`) under the correct cloud model. All maps share the colour scale of
$Z$, and all errors share one diverging scale. The box mean of each map is in its title. A single
day shows how each estimator builds its answer, not how well it does on average; that is the next
section.

**Mean field.** Each fit's $\hat\mu(\cdot, t^*)$ next to the true $\mu$. OLS and GLS vary only with
latitude, as their basis allows. The GLS + $\log\hat q$ fit also follows the $\hat q$ pattern, so
it is warmer where floats are expected to gather.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Top: the true mean field and the three fitted mean fields on one day. Bottom: their errors, mapped and as a zonal mean by latitude."
_show_fig(mf.plot_mean_maps(st))
```

**Mean field + kriging.** Kriging adds the anomaly near the floats. Where floats are dense the
three maps agree and follow the eddies. In the gaps they fall back to their own mean field, so
the mean-field errors above survive there.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Top: the true field with that day's floats, and the kriging map built on each mean field. Bottom: map errors, mapped and as a zonal mean by latitude."
_show_fig(mf.plot_krige_maps(st))
```

**Cross-fit DR.** Top row: the map term, the mixture
$\sum_f (q_f/q)\,\hat m^{(-f)}$ of the $60$ leave-one-float-out maps. Each float's own map is used
where that float was expected to be, so the mixture is close to the kriging map but never lets a
float check itself. Bottom row: each float's check $Z_i - \hat m^{(-f)}(x_i)$, coloured by the
residual and sized by its weight $1/q$, over the faint error of the mixed map. Isolated floats
far from the crowd get the largest weights: the northern floats are
`{python} f"{(st['xy'][:, 1] > 0).mean():.0%}"` of the floats on this day but carry
`{python} f"{st['weight'][st['xy'][:, 1] > 0].sum() / st['weight'].sum():.0%}"` of the weight. The weighted sum of the checks is the correction
added to the map term.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Top: weight of each float's check, and the mixed leave-one-out map for each mean fit. Bottom: map error by latitude, and each float's residual against its own leave-one-out map (size: weight)."
_show_fig(mf.plot_dr_maps(st))
```

## Results under the correct cloud model

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Error of the box-mean estimate over 30 replicates and about 49 target days each, correct cloud model."
_show_fig(mf.plot_errors(df))
```

```{python}
HTML(fmt(mf.summary(dc)))
```

`bias` and `sd` are the mean and standard deviation of the error over all replicate-days. `se` is
the Monte Carlo standard error of the bias, computed from the $30$ replicate-level mean errors, and
`bias_over_se` compares the two.

- **Mean field alone.** The bias falls from `{python} f"{b('mean field only', 'ols'):+.3f}"` (OLS) to
  `{python} f"{b('mean field only', 'gls'):+.3f}"` (GLS) to
  `{python} f"{b('mean field only', 'glsq'):+.3f}"` (GLS + $\log\hat q$), against
  `{python} f"{s.loc[('simple mean of profiles', ''), 'bias']:+.3f}"` for the simple mean of a
  snapshot's profiles. Most of the simple mean's bias is latitude, which any of the mean fits
  absorbs.
- **After kriging.** Kriging repairs much of the OLS mean in the dense south, so OLS and GLS end up
  similar (`{python} f"{b('mean field + kriging', 'ols'):+.3f}"` and
  `{python} f"{b('mean field + kriging', 'gls'):+.3f}"`). The bias that remains is in the sparse
  north, where the map reverts to the mean field (table below). The $\log\hat q$ fit changes the
  mean field there and gives `{python} f"{b('mean field + kriging', 'glsq'):+.3f}"`.
- **Cross-fit DR.** With leave-one-float-out cross-fitting, all three DR estimators are within $2$ Monte Carlo
  standard errors of zero: `{python} f"{b(DR, 'ols'):+.4f}"` (OLS map),
  `{python} f"{b(DR, 'gls'):+.4f}"` (GLS map) and `{python} f"{b(DR, 'glsq'):+.4f}"`
  (GLS + $\log\hat q$ map). Under the correct cloud model the map hardly matters, because the
  correction is exact up to the error in $\hat q$. The price is variance. The DR sd
  (`{python} f"{s.loc[(DR, mf.FIT_LAB['glsq']), 'sd']:.3f}"`) is almost twice that of the
  GLS + $\log\hat q$ kriging map (`{python} f"{s.loc[(KR, mf.FIT_LAB['glsq']), 'sd']:.3f}"`), so per
  target day the kriging map has the lower RMSE
  (`{python} f"{s.loc[(KR, mf.FIT_LAB['glsq']), 'rmse']:.3f}"` against
  `{python} f"{s.loc[(DR, mf.FIT_LAB['glsq']), 'rmse']:.3f}"`). The sd is per target day and averages
  down over many days, but a bias does not.

The DR biases stay within $\pm 0.002$ of zero in every season, so the annual figure is not hiding

cold season. Across replicates, $\hat\gamma$ is
`{python} f"{gam[gam.scenario == 'correct'].gamma.mean():.3f}"`
(sd `{python} f"{gam[gam.scenario == 'correct'].gamma.std():.3f}"`).

## Misspecified cloud models

The real floats always move in the true flow. The clouds, and so $\hat q$, are now drawn from four
wrong models, the same ones as in [the toy report](simex.qmd):

- the weak drift toward warm water is left out;
- the eddies are displaced by a quarter wavelength;
- the cloud noise is too small ($K/4$);
- the cloud noise is too large ($4K$).

The wrong $\hat q$ enters the $\log\hat q$ covariate, the mixing weights $q_f/q$, the residual
weights $1/q$, and the covered set. The OLS and GLS maps do not use $\hat q$, so for them only the
DR correction changes.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Bias of the three DR estimators (filled) and of the GLS + log q-hat kriging map (open), under each cloud model. Bars: 95% Monte Carlo intervals."
_show_fig(mf.plot_scenarios(df))
```

```{python}
t = sc[(sc.stage == DR) | ((sc.stage == KR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB["glsq"]))]
t = t.assign(scenario=t.scenario.map(mf.sx.SCEN_LAB))
HTML(fmt(t[["scenario", "stage", "fit", "bias", "se", "bias_over_se", "sd", "rmse"]]))
```

With a wrong cloud model, DR is no longer unbiased. Its bias is then the product term: the map's
residuals times the error in $\hat q$. The quality of the map starts to matter.

- **Drift omitted, or noise too large.** The clouds no longer concentrate where floats actually
  gather, so the weights are too flat and the correction is too small. DR removes roughly a third to
  a half of the kriging bias. The $\log\hat q$ map is the best of the three in both cases
  (`{python} f"{bs('no_conv', DR, 'glsq'):+.4f}"` and `{python} f"{bs('K_large', DR, 'glsq'):+.4f}"`).
- **Eddies displaced.** $\hat q$ is high in the wrong places, so the covariate carries almost no
  information ($\hat\gamma$ falls to
  `{python} f"{gam[gam.scenario == 'shifted'].gamma.mean():.3f}"`), and the three DR estimators end
  up similar (`{python} f"{bs('shifted', DR, 'ols'):+.4f}"` to
  `{python} f"{bs('shifted', DR, 'glsq'):+.4f}"`), still below the kriging maps.
- **Noise too small.** This is the dangerous direction. Clouds that are too tight give floats
  landing in their thin tails very large weights, so DR over-corrects. On the OLS and GLS maps the
  bias becomes `{python} f"{bs('K_small', DR, 'ols'):+.4f}"`, larger in size than the uncorrected
  kriging bias and of the opposite sign. On the $\log\hat q$ map, whose residuals are small, the
  over-correction shrinks to `{python} f"{bs('K_small', DR, 'glsq'):+.4f}"`. Coverage also drops to
  `{python} f"{df[df.scenario == 'K_small'].cover.mean():.0%}"` on average.

Across all five cloud models, the largest absolute bias of DR on the GLS + $\log\hat q$ map is
`{python} f"{sc[(sc.stage == DR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB['glsq'])].bias.abs().max():.4f}"`, against
`{python} f"{sc[(sc.stage == DR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB['ols'])].bias.abs().max():.4f}"` for DR on
the OLS map and
`{python} f"{sc[(sc.stage == KR) & (sc.fit == mf.FIT_LAB['glsq'])].bias.abs().max():.4f}"` for the
GLS + $\log\hat q$ kriging map alone. A good map limits how much a wrong $\hat q$ can hurt. And
since too little cloud noise costs more than too much, the noise should be calibrated, or erred on
the wide side.

**Not included here.** The covariance is oracle. An Argo-only version would estimate $K$ from the
profiles, which preferential sampling also biases. That affects only the maps, not the validity
argument for the DR step.
